title: This week's learning objectives
html:
This week’s question: how do we know what works?

Last week’s claim was that some ways of helping do far more good than others. That is only useful if you can tell which is which, and intuition is a poor guide.

This week you learn how charity evaluators do it. A cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA) estimates how much good an intervention does per euro. You don’t need to build one to give well, because evaluators like GiveWell do that for you. You learn how they work so that you can judge how far to trust a figure like “$5,000 per life saved” and see where the judgement calls are.

By the end of this week, you will be able to:

  • Read a charity evaluation critically and find the weakest link in its reasoning

  • Place evidence on the hierarchy of reliability, from RCTs to testimonials

  • Follow a cost-effectiveness model and see where judgement calls enter

  • Explain how moral weights shape which interventions get funded

  • Build a simple cost-effectiveness estimate from a handful of inputs

  • Engage with critiques of the evidence-based approach, including questions of power and perspective

Time commitment

  • Reading: about 65 minutes (course text, Singer chapter, two GiveWell pieces, Karnofsky blog post)

  • Quiz: about 10 minutes

  • Workbook: about 60 minutes

  • Total before the session: about 2–2.5 hours

Do the reading first, then the quiz, then the workbook. Bring your completed workbook to the session.
